processing: Dried limes (noomi Basra) are cracked into pieces or pricked, seeded and simmered in water for 15 to 30 minutes, then strained and sweetened.
harvest_season: Not seasonal. It is made from stored dried limes throughout the year.
appearance_dry: Hard, hollow whole dried limes, light in the hand, in shades of tan to dark brown.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber, typical of a long-simmered citrus peel.
appearance_wet: Softened dark pieces of lime peel, strained out before serving.
taste_profile: Very sour and aromatic with a tart citrus edge, turning mildly sweet depending on the sugar.

brewing.notes: Crack or prick two limes, a rough quantity, and simmer for 15 to 30 minutes. Strain, then sweeten with sugar or honey; saffron is an occasional addition.

vintage_note: There are no vintages or harvest years. Dried limes are sold whole by weight in spice shops, and Omani limes are a named style. As with other dried spices, buy from a shop with quick turnover.
description:
Dried lime tea is a sour, aromatic infusion of dried limes, traditional to Iraq and the Arabian Peninsula and widely drunk in Kuwait, Oman and the United Arab Emirates. The Iraqi name, chai noomi basra, refers to the dried limes themselves.

The limes need breaking open. Crack them or prick them, remove the seeds and simmer the peels for 15 to 30 minutes. A quick steep won't extract much from a hard dried fruit.

The cup is strikingly sour and needs some sugar or honey to balance it. Saffron threads are a good addition when you want something more special. It is served hot.

It is also a home remedy for indigestion, upset stomach, diarrhoea and nausea. Buy whole limes rather than powder if you want a clean cup, and note that Omani limes are prized for their pleasant tartness.
history:
The drink is documented as a household tradition of Iraq and the Gulf, with noomi Basra in its Iraqi name. No reliable date or originator is recorded for it.

Its use as a stomach remedy continues alongside its role as an everyday hot drink.
